broader_review_uses.material: The paper describes how nucleotides are primarily intracellular and how extracellular purines are typically parent forms due to phosphatase activity. It notes that plasma contamination is minimized by the strong ion exchange step.
broader_review_uses.purpose: To illustrate the complexity of measuring intracellular signaling molecules (like ATP/ADP ratios) which are often implicated in immune checkpoint regulation. Highlights that accurate measurement requires careful separation from extracellular contaminants.

broader_review_uses.material: Explains that PBMCs have higher nucleotide levels because they are nucleated cells performing de novo synthesis, while RBCs rely on salvage pathways and use nucleotides primarily for energy.
broader_review_uses.purpose: To provide a biological rationale for why different blood cell types have vastly different metabolic profiles. This supports discussions on why PBMCs are the preferred matrix for studying immune-related metabolic changes in cancer immunotherapy.

facet_contributions.boundaries: Does not measure nucleotides in gut tissue or directly link them to ICI efficacy. Focuses on healthy/infected baseline states rather than treatment-induced changes related to immunotherapy.
facet_contributions.contribution: Provides baseline physiological data on the relative concentrations of ATP, GTP, and ITP in PBMCs versus RBCs (10x, 55x, and 5.6x higher in PBMCs, respectively). This establishes the expected magnitude of intracellular nucleotide pools in immune-relevant cells (PBMCs) compared to other blood components.
facet_contributions.possible_uses: Can be used to contextualize the scale of nucleotide changes observed in studies linking microbiome metabolites to immune cell function. Helps define the 'normal' range or ratio of these nucleotides in the target cell type (PBMCs) for solid tumor immune responses.

facet_contributions.boundaries: Specific to purine nucleotides; does not address other microbial metabolites (e.g., SCFAs, bile acids) often linked to ICI response. Does not explain the mechanism of microbiome modulation, only the analytical constraints of measuring host metabolites.
facet_contributions.contribution: Details the chemical instability of triphosphates in Dried Blood Spots (DBS), showing a 26% decrease in TP and 184% increase in MP due to hydrolysis during drying/storage. Identifies environmental contamination as a major confounder for low-abundance nucleotides.
facet_contributions.possible_uses: Useful for discussing methodological pitfalls in measuring intracellular metabolites in clinical trials. If any studies in the review use DBS for metabolite profiling, this paper serves as a cautionary example regarding sample handling and potential artifacts in nucleotide data.

planning_summary: This paper provides a detailed analytical methodology for quantifying purine nucleotides (ATP, GTP, ITP and their MP forms) in human blood cells. While it does not directly address gut microbiome or immune checkpoint inhibitors, it offers valuable technical context for understanding the measurement of intracellular metabolites that may influence immune responses. It also highlights the biological differences in nucleotide pools between nucleated (PBMCs) and non-nucleated (RBCs) cells, and identifies stability challenges in common clinical sampling matrices like DBS.
scope_interpretation_cautions: This paper is a methodological study, not a clinical outcome study regarding ICI efficacy or microbiome composition.
The 'hydrolysis' finding in DBS is specific to the drying/storage conditions described; it does not imply all DBS samples fail, but highlights a risk factor.
Contamination issues are specific to the sensitivity of the assay and environmental factors; they do not invalidate the method but require strict controls.
Do not extrapolate the nucleotide concentration ratios (PBMC/RBC) to other tissues or disease states without evidence.
title: A LC-MS/MS method for quantifying adenosine, guanosine and inosine nucleotides in human cells
